lessons.body:
# Imports and the module system

Any `.py` file is a module. `import` loads it once and binds it to a name; `from ... import ...` pulls specific names out of it.

```python
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))        # 4.0

from math import sqrt, pi
print(sqrt(16), pi)         # 4.0 3.141592653589793

import math as m             # alias, common for long names
from datetime import datetime as dt
```

When you `import x`, Python searches `sys.path` — roughly: the script's directory, then installed packages, then the standard library. That's why a file named `math.py` in your project would shadow the real `math` module and break everything: never name your files after standard-library modules.

```python
import sys
print(sys.path)   # where Python looks for modules, in order
```

Circular imports (a imports b, b imports a) are the classic beginner trap. They usually mean the shared code belongs in a third module both can import. If you hit an `ImportError` that only happens in one import order, suspect a cycle.

`from package import *` dumps every public name into your namespace. It's fine in an interactive session; in real code it hides where names come from and risks collisions. Prefer explicit imports — they're grep-able and honest about dependencies.
lessons.jsNote: Java: `import math` is like `import static java.lang.Math.*` except it doesn't pollute your namespace — you still say `math.sqrt()`. There's no classpath to configure; `sys.path` is the classpath and it includes your script's directory by default. JavaScript (ES modules): `import { sqrt } from './math.js'` looks similar, but Python imports resolve at runtime against `sys.path`, not at build time — and unlike ESM's live bindings, `from x import y` copies the reference at import time.
keyPoints: Every `.py` file is a module; `import` runs it once and caches it in `sys.modules`.
`import x`, `from x import y`, `import x as z` — prefer explicit over `import *`.
Python searches `sys.path` (script dir, installed packages, stdlib); don't name files after stdlib modules.
Circular imports signal that shared code needs its own module.
lessons.title: Imports and the module system

lessons.body:
# The standard library tour

Python ships with "batteries included": a large standard library covering most everyday needs without installing anything. You won't memorize it — you'll learn to recognize which drawer to open.

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

now = datetime.now()
print(now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))        # 2026-10-08
deadline = now + timedelta(days=7)     # date arithmetic just works
```

Modules you'll reach for constantly: `os` and `sys` (environment, argv, exit codes), `json` (you met it in File I/O), `re` (regular expressions), `math`/`statistics`, `random`, `collections` (`Counter`, `defaultdict`, `deque`), `itertools` (you'll meet it properly in Intermediate Python), and `dataclasses`.

```python
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

votes = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "b"]
print(Counter(votes))            # Counter({'a': 3, 'b': 2, 'c': 1})

groups = defaultdict(list)       # missing keys auto-create an empty list
for name, team in [("amy", "red"), ("bo", "blue"), ("cy", "red")]:
    groups[team].append(name)
print(dict(groups))             # {'red': ['amy', 'cy'], 'blue': ['bo']}
```

`Counter` and `defaultdict` deserve special attention because they eliminate the tedious "check if the key exists first" pattern that litters beginner code. Whenever you catch yourself writing `if key not in d: d[key] = ...`, there's probably a stdlib tool for it.

The docs at docs.python.org/3/library are the reference you'll actually use in practice. The skill isn't memorization — it's knowing the library is big enough that you check it before writing your own version.
lessons.jsNote: Java: the stdlib is the JDK class library, but flatter — one `import` per module instead of hunting through `java.util` vs `java.time` vs `java.nio`. `Counter` is a multiset (Guava's `Multiset`); `defaultdict` is `Map.computeIfAbsent` as a data structure. JavaScript: Node's built-ins (`fs`, `path`) play this role, but they're far thinner — Python's stdlib is a genuine selling point of the language.
keyPoints: The stdlib covers datetimes, OS interaction, regex, math, randomness, and collections — check it before reinventing.
`Counter` and `defaultdict` remove the manual "initialize the key first" dance.
docs.python.org/3/library is the reference; the skill is knowing what to look up.
lessons.title: The standard library tour

lessons.body:
# pip and virtual environments

The standard library doesn't cover everything, so Python has pip (the package installer) and PyPI (the package index). `pip install requests` fetches and installs a package.

```python
# terminal, not Python:
# pip install requests
```

```python
import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
print(r.status_code)   # 200
print(r.json()["current_user_url"])
```

Never install packages globally if you can avoid it. A virtual environment is an isolated Python installation per project — its own packages, its own versions — so project A's `requests==2.28` never fights project B's `requests==2.31`.

```python
# terminal:
# python3 -m venv .venv        # create the environment in .venv/
# source .venv/bin/activate    # activate it (prompt shows (.venv))
# pip install requests         # now installs INTO .venv, not globally
# pip freeze > requirements.txt  # snapshot exact versions
# deactivate                   # leave the environment
```

`requirements.txt` is the contract: anyone who clones your project runs `pip install -r requirements.txt` inside a fresh venv and gets your exact dependencies. Commit it; don't commit `.venv/` itself (it's big and machine-specific — add it to `.gitignore`).

The failure mode this prevents is real: two projects needing two versions of one library, or a tutorial's code breaking because your global environment drifted. One venv per project, created at project start, is the habit.
lessons.jsNote: Java: pip is Maven Central/Gradle's dependency step combined — but there's no `pom.xml`; `requirements.txt` is the flat list of pinned versions. A venv is per-project isolation the way Maven's local repo tries to be, except it also isolates the interpreter itself. JavaScript: pip = npm, PyPI = npm registry, `requirements.txt` is roughly `package.json` dependencies (flat, no lockfile semantics — that's what `pip freeze` output or poetry adds), and a venv is exactly `node_modules` isolation done at the interpreter level.
keyPoints: `pip install <package>` installs from PyPI; `pip install -r requirements.txt` reproduces an environment.
A venv (`.venv`) isolates a project's packages — one per project.
Activate with `source .venv/bin/activate`; snapshot with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`.
lessons.title: pip and virtual environments

lessons.body:
# Scripts, __main__, and project layout

A Python file has two jobs it might do: be imported as a module, or be run as a script. The `__name__ == "__main__"` guard lets one file do both cleanly.

```python
# greet.py
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(greet("world"))
```

When you run `python greet.py`, Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"` and the print executes. When another file does `import greet`, `__name__` is `"greet"`, so the print is skipped — importing stays side-effect free. Rule: a module should never do work on import; put executable code under the guard or inside functions.

```python
# main.py
import greet
print(greet.greet("raymond"))   # importing greet printed nothing. Good.
```

A package is a directory with an `__init__.py` file (it can be empty) — it lets you organize modules into dotted namespaces like `myapp.utils`. A sane small-project layout looks like this:

```python
# myproject/
#   pyproject.toml        # or requirements.txt — project metadata & deps
#   README.md
#   src/myapp/
#       __init__.py
#       __main__.py       # lets you run: python -m myapp
#       utils.py
#   tests/
#       test_utils.py
```

`python -m myapp` runs the package's `__main__.py` with imports resolving correctly — it avoids the classic bug where running a script directly breaks its relative imports. When imports mysteriously fail, check two things: are you running from the project root, and would `-m` fix it.
lessons.jsNote: Java: the `__main__` guard is `public static void main(String[] args)` — the entry point — except in Python any module can have one, and the guard is what keeps it from firing on import. There's no `public`/`private` enforcement (see the OOP module for underscore conventions). JavaScript: this is the `if (require.main === module)` idiom from CommonJS — same idea, far more common in Python.
keyPoints: `if __name__ == "__main__":` separates "run as script" from "imported as module".
Modules must be side-effect free on import — no top-level print/network/IO.
A package is a directory with `__init__.py`; `python -m pkg` runs its `__main__.py`.
Keep a boring, standard layout: source under `src/`, tests under `tests/`, deps pinned.
lessons.title: Scripts, __main__, and project layout
